title: Detect Adversary-in-the-Middle via Network and Configuration Anomalies
shortTitle: Detect Adversary-in-the-Middle via Network and Configurat...
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) activity, where an attacker inserts themselves between a client and a server to read or alter traffic. It is mapped to technique T1557 and matters because a successful AiTM position defeats encryption in practice: session cookies, credentials and authentication codes can be relayed or captured even when the protocol is encrypted end to end. The telemetry that makes detection possible is the combination of network protocol anomalies (rogue Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, or DHCP, servers, unexpected Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, replies, unusual Link-Layer Discovery Protocol, or LLDP, and spanning-tree topology changes), host configuration changes (new root certificates, proxy settings, name resolution or routing changes) and authentication events that suddenly arrive from a new network location. In practice the main failure mode is noise and blindness: AiTM often produces no single dramatic event, so the detection depends on correlating weak signals within a short window, and if certificate inventory, Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol snooping or wireless controller logs are not collected, most of the pattern is invisible.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for signs that someone has quietly placed themselves in the middle of your network traffic. It watches for strange network answers. One example is a second device that claims to hand out network settings. It also watches for sudden changes to trust settings on a computer. Together those signs suggest traffic may be passing through an attacker instead of going straight to its destination.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an attacker sits in the middle, your encryption does not protect you fully. The attacker can copy a login session and use it later. They may not even need your password. On a normal day nobody adds new trust settings or answers network requests. Catching these small changes early can stop a full account takeover.
howItWorks: Network devices and switches send records about address lookups, address claims and link changes to your central logging system.
The rule looks for a claim that should come from one device only, but now comes from several. Two different devices may answer the same address request.
On the hosts, the rule watches trust stores, proxy settings and name resolution settings for unexpected changes.
It also watches authentication records for successful logins from a new network address soon after one of those network events.
It joins these records by time and by network segment, usually within a short window of a few minutes.
If a network anomaly and a configuration change appear together, the system raises one alert for an analyst to review.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk that hands out room keys. A stranger stands beside the desk and starts handing out their own keys. Guests still get into their rooms, but the stranger now knows every room number. The night manager would notice two people giving out keys at one desk. That is what this rule watches for, plus the moment a guest's key stops working.
takeaways: Adversary-in-the-middle means an attacker quietly sits between two systems and copies or changes what passes by.
One strange network event is usually not enough. The rule looks for a network change plus a trust or login change.
You need switch, address and certificate records to see this, so check that those sources are really collected.

objectives: Explain what an adversary-in-the-middle position is and how it changes the value of stolen session data.
Identify the network telemetry sources that reveal rogue network service answers on your segments.
Recognise host-side trust changes, such as new root certificates or proxy settings, as AiTM indicators.
Correlate a network anomaly with a later authentication event from an unexpected network address.
List the collection gaps that would leave this detection blind in your own environment.
Describe how to tune the rule so normal network churn does not create daily alerts.
dataSources: Network infrastructure syslog from switches and wireless controllers, including Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol snooping, Address Resolution Protocol inspection and spanning-tree topology change events
Windows Security event 4624 successful logon with logon type and source workstation and source network address
Windows endpoint telemetry for root certificate store installs and proxy or name resolution configuration changes, such as the certificate store change records published by the Windows event log
Sysmon event 22 DNS query and Sysmon event 3 network connection for hosts that report name resolution and connection metadata
Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory Federation Services sign-in logs carrying device, network address and session token details
logic: The pattern to detect is a short-lived cluster in which the network fabric reports a service that should be unique now answering from more than one device, or a link or topology change that redirects traffic, and a host on the same segment shows a fresh trust or resolution change or a successful authentication from a new network address. The fields that must be correlated are the network segment or switch port, the MAC and IP address pairs, the timestamps, and the host identifier in the endpoint or authentication records. The benign case is a scheduled network change, a failover of a legitimate second address service, or an approved certificate deployment, all of which appear in change records or affect many hosts at once. The malicious case is narrow: one segment, one or two hosts, an unmanaged device answering a network request, and an authentication that arrives moments later from a location the account has never used.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Possible Adversary-in-the-Middle Network and Trust Anomaly
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection_dhcp:
#     event_type: 'dhcp_offer'
#     server_count: '>1'
#   selection_arp:
#     event_type: 'arp_reply'
#     duplicate_ip_claim: true
#   selection_host:
#     event_type: 'root_certificate_install'
#   timeframe: 10m
#   condition: (selection_dhcp or selection_arp) and selection_host
# level: high
falsePositives: A redundant or failover address service that briefly answers alongside the primary server during a planned maintenance window
Virtualisation or container host networking that generates duplicate address claims when a virtual machine is live migrated
Enterprise certificate management tooling that pushes a new internal root certificate to a maintenance group overnight
Wireless roaming between access points that logs link and topology changes for the same client device
A network troubleshooting session where an engineer runs a temporary packet capture or transparent proxy on a lab segment
tuningNotes: Start by baselining which devices are allowed to answer address and name resolution requests on each segment, then filter out those authorised addresses and any planned change windows from the change management feed. Scope the rule to user and server segments rather than lab, guest or voice networks, where duplicate claims are routine. Add a filter for approved certificate deployment jobs by signer or by publisher so that a mass rollout does not flood the queue, and require the endpoint anomaly to involve a single host rather than many hosts at once, because wide impact usually means management tooling. Keep a lower-severity variant that alerts on the network anomaly alone so you retain visibility when host telemetry is missing, and accept that narrowing by segment will lose coverage of any rogue device that is plugged into an unmanaged or guest network you chose to exclude.
